title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.

context_blocks.text: Decision trees describe classification through simple successive tests of individual input bits. A small tree may nevertheless hide complicated interactions among the variables. The question asks whether uniform random observations suffice for efficient prediction, even when the learner is free to return a representation different from a tree.

At a fixed node bound, the number of tree descriptions is at most exponential in a polynomial in the size and logarithm of the input dimension. Consequently the realizable information-theoretic sample requirement is polynomial in size, dimension and inverse error. The desired theorem concerns computation as well as data, rather than mere statistical identifiability.

A tree with at most \(s\) nodes has at most \(s\) leaves and can be expressed as a DNF with at most \(s\) terms. Known uniform-example DNF learners therefore provide quasipolynomial algorithms in the polynomial-size regime, as summarized by Servedio’s Theorem 13. That is a useful general upper bound, but a dimension exponent growing logarithmically with size or inverse error is not the requested one fixed polynomial.

Kalai–Teng’s Theorem 1 learns every target tree efficiently for most product distributions obtained by randomly perturbing their coordinate means by a fixed positive amount. Its probability is over both the perturbation and the training examples. The exact vector of uniform means is a particular unperturbed point, so success for almost all perturbed means does not imply the guarantee at that point. The theorem is explicitly improper and outputs a polynomial threshold function.

The ITCS 2025 source again states that efficient uniform-PAC learning of polynomial-size trees is unknown in the sample-only model. Its positive backdoor-defense theorem gives the defender the represented tree, which allows direct examination and evaluation. That observation model differs from receiving only labeled examples of a hidden tree. A fast detector with the representation supplied is not a PAC learner for this card.

Membership queries make uniform decision-tree learning easier because they provide labels at chosen inputs. Proper-learning problems impose a different restriction by requiring a tree output. This target has the passive observation interface and permits arbitrary Boolean circuit output; hardness for a restricted output class cannot be transferred just by matching the words “decision tree learning.”

The checked May 2026 paper on product spaces explicitly allows label queries at arbitrary inputs in §3. Its main size bound also depends on the optimal tree’s maximum and average depths and can be quasipolynomial even for logarithmic-depth trees. These are useful guarantees for the studied greedy procedure, but neither the interface nor the bound supplies the full polynomial sample-only learner.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.

why: Settle the sample-only computational learnability of a canonical interpretable Boolean model.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.

progress.text: Kalai–Teng give a polynomial-time improper learner with high probability over perturbed product-distribution means, while explicitly retaining the fixed uniform-example question.
The backdoor-defense paper restates the sample-only question and proves a representation-aware defense theorem with a different input interface.
Servedio’s survey records the quasipolynomial uniform DNF upper bound and the junta obstacle for fully polynomial learning.
Decision Tree Learning on Product Spaces analyzes a query-based greedy learner with depth-dependent output size; §3 explicitly supplies chosen-input labels.

source_formulation.text: Can every polynomial-size Boolean decision tree be learned in polynomial time from independent uniformly random labeled examples, with no restriction that the output remain a tree?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

sentences: The card asks for a polynomial-time learner for every small Boolean decision tree from independent uniform labeled examples.
The tree is hidden and the learner receives neither chosen-input labels nor its representation.
A successful learner may return any efficient Boolean circuit with the requested prediction error and two-thirds confidence.
Known smoothed, query-based and representation-aware results provide different guarantees and do not settle this passive learning target.
The completed card preserves its importance and scope while making the accuracy encoding, resource bounds and full Lean proof criterion explicit.
